column3: 1,439 rows are exact copies of another row (all 6 columns identical); 95,939 unique order_ids in 97,378 rows. Copies with the same id but different values: 0.
column4: Dropped the second copy of each. Because every copy is identical there is no 'which version is right' question.
column5: Without this, each duplicated COD order counts twice in both numerator and denominator.

column3: payment_type values for COD: 'cod' (48,723), 'Cash on Delivery' (3,398), 'COD' (3,342). Every store uses all three (about 12% of each store's COD orders are not 'cod').
column4: Treated 'cod', 'COD' and 'Cash on Delivery' as COD (trim + lower-case, explicit allow-list).
column5: Filtering on 'cod' alone would drop 6,740 COD orders, spread across every store.

column2: Status written in 20 different ways (case + stray spaces)
column3: 20 raw spellings for 5 real statuses, e.g. 'delivered', 'DELIVERED', ' Delivered', 'rto', 'RTO', ' Rto'. 7,446 values have a leading/trailing space.
column4: Trimmed and lower-cased; checked the result is exactly {delivered, rto, cancelled, in_transit, pending}.
column5: An exact match on 'rto'/'delivered' would silently drop 5,623 of 47,664 final COD orders (12%).

column2: Test merchants mixed in with real stores
column3: M_TEST_01 and M_TEST_02: 1,686 orders, COD-only (payment types: ['cod']), COD return rates 88-89%, both above the 200-order bar. So the brief's '26 stores' is really 24 stores + 2 test accounts.
column5: Kept in, they would be #1 and #2 in the store ranking, and the overall rate would read 30.20% instead of 28.37% (+1.83 points).

column2: Timestamps are UTC, the weeks must be IST
column3: All timestamps end in 'Z' (UTC). In IST the data spans exactly Mon 27 Jul 00:00 to Sun 25 Oct 23:59 (13 full weeks), which confirms the stamps really are UTC. 230 orders carry a UTC date of 26 Jul.
column4: Converted every timestamp to Asia/Kolkata before assigning days and weeks.
column5: Bucketing on the raw UTC date would invent a 14th week (20 Jul) with 230 orders and shift every order placed 00:00-05:29 IST into the previous day.

column3: 283 orders have an empty created_at (147 of them are COD with a final outcome). Order ids track time almost perfectly (rank correlation 0.9999).
column4: Placed each in the week of its neighbouring order ids. Checked on 93,970 dated orders first: when both neighbours share a week the guess is right 100.00% of the time. All 283 undated orders had agreeing neighbours. They count fully in the store ranking, which needs no date.
column5: Dropping them instead changes no weekly rate by more than 0.11 points.

column2: Two whole days have no orders at all
column3: No order is dated Mon 14 Sep, Tue 15 Sep (every other day has 908-1,217). Order ids run without a gap straight across them, so the orders were never recorded rather than deleted afterwards. The week of 14 Sep therefore has only 5 days (about 30% fewer orders).
column4: Not filled in (there is nothing to recover). The week's rate is still reported but flagged 'partial: 5 of 7 days'.
column5: A rate is a ratio, so it stays comparable. The week's volume is not, and should not be read as a demand drop.

column2: COD orders still 'pending' / 'in_transit' weeks or months later
column3: 4,376 COD orders never reached a final outcome; 3,175 of them were placed before 1 Oct, and orders from July are still 'in transit'. The share is flat (about 8% every week), so these look like statuses that stopped updating rather than parcels genuinely still moving.
column4: Excluded from the denominator, as the definition says (no final outcome). Bounded their possible effect instead.
column5: If every stale order were really a return, weekly rates would rise by up to 6.75 points and the top 3 would read M122, M108, M112 - #1 and #2 hold, but #3 is not robust to this data problem.

column4: Excluded: a cancellation is not a delivery outcome, so it is neither a return nor a delivery.
column5: Counting them as 'not returned' would wrongly lower the overall rate from 28.37% to 26.53%.

column2: Store M117 is too small to rank
column3: Only 145 COD orders with a final outcome (and 227 orders in total, about 18 a week). Its 63.5% return rate would rank #1 among real stores, but the 95% range is 55-71%.
column4: Excluded from the ranking by the >= 200 rule. Still included in the weekly rates.
column5: A naive 'top 3 by rate' would put this store first.

column3: 3 orders have order_value = 9,999,999 (ORD0030525, ORD0031256, ORD0039939); every other order is between 121 and 13,421.
column4: Kept the orders (status and payment are fine) but flagged the value as unusable.
column5: No effect on return rates, which count orders. Would distort any revenue or AOV figure.

column2: Other things checked and found clean
column3: CRLF line endings (handled by the CSV reader); every row has 6 fields; no non-numeric, zero or negative values; no store has a different currency or unit (median order 1,069-1,137 for every store); no near-duplicate double-submits (same store + same value within 10 minutes); 1,073 prepaid orders were also returned (normal for undeliverable parcels; out of scope since the question is about COD).
